chunks: From him, from Abdullah Al-Hajjal, from Abu Uthman Al-Qabousy, from the one who mentioned him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, lent to His enemies manners from the manners of His friends, so that His friends may live among His enemies in their dominion. And in another report: 'And were it not for that, they would not have left a friend of Allah except that they would have killed him.'

key_terms.أَعَارَ: Lent or borrowed (metaphorically granting a temporary trait)
key_terms.أَوْلِيَائِهِ: His friends (plural of wali, referring to God's close servants)
key_terms.دَوْلَاتِهِمْ: Their dominion, rule, or periods of power
key_terms.وَلِيّاً لِلَّهِ: A friend of God (singular of awliya)

ai.seo_question: Why did God give enemies of the faithful some of the good manners of the faithful?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the divine wisdom of 'I'ara' (lending) good manners to the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt, a concept central to Shia political theology explaining the endurance of the righteous amidst hostile powers. Scholars note that this shared virtue prevents the immediate eradication of the Awliya, allowing them to fulfill their role as guides within the broader society. The second part of the narration underscores the fragility of this tolerance, highlighting that without this divine concession, the hostility of the enemies would have led to the swift elimination of every single friend of God.
